description: My name, Setareh, means star, so a career looking down from space was kind of inevitable. After a slightly confusing detour through Civil Engineering, my first NASA image during my master’s showed me my path. Now I’m a PhD candidate in Environmental Sciences in Canada, using satellite data for sustainable agriculture, with a stop at Planet Lab to watch satellites get built, launched and turned into data. Little me would be thrilled. 🛰️🌱
summary:
Every fall, a farmer decides what goes on each field next year, and whether the soil will be bare when the spring storms come. FieldSense helps from space: NASA satellites have watched every field in Canada for years, and FieldSense turns each field’s history into a barcode, brown when the soil is bare and green when roots are holding it.
Why I built it: satellites amaze me every time I think about them. Then I think about farmers, who weigh so many factors with only limited information, while they feed so many people. That is a huge responsibility, and we should help make it less overwhelming. Farms and satellites, isn’t that a cool combination? So why not ask satellites for help with these big decisions?
FieldSense reads every clear NASA HLS image of a field, corrects NASA POWER weather with the nearest Environment Canada station, and builds 1,000 possible 2027 seasons to show the risks. Then it compares rotations side by side, and the farmer decides what matters most. Click your field on the website’s satellite map, and in 5–10 minutes the app shows its history from space, its 2027 weather and, for corn, soybean and wheat fields, which rotation and why.
At the Elora Research Station’s rotation experiment, the diverse rotation kept living cover on 39% of off-season days, the simple one on 3%. On 42 farm fields in five provinces, diverse fields were less bare too.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

FieldSense answers one question for a farm field: which crop rotation should come next, and how risky is next season? It works in five steps:

  1. Find fields anywhere in Canada. For a location, FieldSense finds farm fields within 5 km on Canada's 30 m crop map (AAFC Annual Crop Inventory). It groups them with one rule that works in every province: simple rotations have at most two crops and no forage (corn–soybean, canola–wheat, wheat–fallow), diverse rotations have three or more crops or hay in the rotation.
  2. Read every field from space. I use every clear NASA HLS image since 2021 (Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2, 30 m) and turn each field's greenness into a "barcode": one row per year, brown when the soil is bare and green when plants are growing. From when the field is green, FieldSense reads the type of crop (winter cereal, spring crop like wheat or canola, summer crop like corn or soybean, forage, or fallow), and it measures the soil cover: bare days in the season, bare days in spring storm season, and green days outside summer.
  3. Look at next season. It downloads 30 years of NASA POWER weather for the location, finds the nearest Environment Canada station with a long record by itself, and corrects POWER with it, month by month. At Elora, POWER was about 1 °C too warm, and after the correction the bias is about 0.1 °C on years I kept aside for testing. Then it builds 1,000 possible seasons for 2027 and counts how many bring a late frost, a heavy storm on bare soil, heat or a dry spell.
  4. Compare and let the farmer decide. Rotations are compared side by side on soil cover, climate risk and how many crops to manage. There is no single score: on the website you move sliders for what matters to you, and the ranking changes right away.
  5. Try your own field. On the website, a farmer zooms in on a satellite map and clicks on their field. The FieldSense web app (Hugging Face) opens with that location and starts by itself, with no login. It finds the field at that exact point on the crop map and, in about 5–10 minutes, shows its crops and satellite barcode, its soil cover, the 2027 weather from the nearest station, and which rotation and why. If the point is a town, water or forest, it says so. Nothing is stored.

How I know it works. The main test is the Elora Research Station's long-term rotation experiment in Ontario. There, both rotations grow side by side on the same land, so the rotation is the only difference. Over 10 years read from space, the crops matched the field records, and the diverse rotation had living cover on 39% of off-season days against 3% for the simple one. Then I checked FieldSense on 42 real farm fields it had never seen, in six locations in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec. I set the pass rule before looking at the results (at least 80% agreement with Canada's crop map), and all six passed: 177 of 210 field-years (84%). The crop map is also made from satellites, so this is agreement with the best map we have, not ground truth. Diverse fields were less bare in all six locations, 7 points of the season on average (90% interval 1 to 13), but with 6 to 8 fields per location the difference is clear on its own only in Saskatchewan and Ontario. These are real farms, not an experiment, and they can differ in other ways too, so I see them as showing the same pattern as Elora, not as proof by themselves.

What benefits does it have?

  • A farmer or an advisor sees the real history of fields in their area, the odds for next season and a clear comparison, from free NASA data, without sensors or field visits.
  • It shows soil cover as something you can see, not only a number: the barcode, the "Watch a year" satellite animation and four key moments (spring storms, early summer, late summer, after harvest) show a simple field bare in spring and after harvest while a diverse one stays green.
  • Every number says how much you can trust it (measured, validated, modelled or assumed), so a farmer knows what is solid and what to check locally.
  • It found something useful about Canada: in Ontario and Quebec, diverse rotations triple the living cover outside summer (30% vs 10%, 32% vs 6%) because of winter wheat and hay, but on the Prairies both groups are almost never green outside summer, because most crops are sown in spring. So the best way to protect soil is different in each region.

What is the intended impact?

Bare soil in spring storms is where topsoil is lost, and with a warmer climate these risks are changing. I want a farmer anywhere in Canada to be able to see how much their fields are left bare, what next season could bring, and which rotation keeps roots in the ground longer, and then decide for themselves. Next steps are rotation options for Prairie crops (canola, spring cereals, pulses), testing it with farmers and crop advisors, more fields per location, adding economics, and a faster web app.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did I use?

Python (numpy, pandas, rasterio, pyproj, shapely, scipy, earthaccess, Pillow) in Google Colab, NASA Earthdata for the satellite data, a Gradio web app on Hugging Face Spaces for "try your own field", pytest with GitHub Actions (85 automatic tests, every change through a pull request), and a static website (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, with a Leaflet satellite map) on GitHub Pages. No special hardware: everything runs on free cloud notebooks and free NASA data.

How is it creative?

  • Most tools estimate soil cover from crop calendars or models. FieldSense measures it on each field from 30 m satellite images, every clear day, and checks itself against Canada's crop map.
  • It reads crops from when a field is green, not from a crop list, so the same method works for corn in Ontario and canola in Saskatchewan.
  • It shows the evidence as pictures (barcodes, Watch a year, key moments) and labels every number with how it was checked.
  • A farmer only has to click on their field on a map: everything else, from the satellite images to the nearest weather station, is found automatically.
  • It doesn't give one answer: it shows the trade-offs, and I tested how much the answer depends on priorities with 2,000 random sets of weights (at Elora, the diverse rotation was best in 89% of them).

What factors did I consider?

  • Honesty about uncertainty: pass rules set before the results, held-out years for the weather correction, intervals on every comparison, and a page section about what we don't know yet.
  • The farmer stays in control: FieldSense supports the decision, it doesn't make it.
  • Privacy: the trial's field records and the farm field outlines stay private. The website only shows aggregate results and locations rounded to about 1 km, and the web app doesn't store anyone's field.
  • Limits I know about: no yield, profit or labour yet; the rotation choice only covers corn, soybean and winter wheat for now (for canola, spring cereals and pulses the app shows the history, soil cover and 2027 weather, and says the rotation options are not ready yet), and the risk thresholds are the Ontario ones; few fields per location, so the intervals are wide; and the crop map doesn't record cover crops. A new field takes about 5–10 minutes in the web app, because it reads every satellite image live.
